name: Nanoneedling / hair microneedle patches

card.summary: Dissolving microneedle patches are a real drug-delivery technology, but no published trial reviewed here tests them for hair growth.
card.note: Published patch studies cover psoriasis, vaccines, insulin and growth hormone, not hair loss.

quick.overview:
Microneedle patches are small arrays of tiny needles, often made of dissolving material, that release a drug into the upper skin layers. The term is used in hair-loss circles for patches said to deliver actives such as minoxidil or growth-factor products to the scalp.
Published research on dissolving patches concerns other uses, such as psoriasis, vaccines, insulin and hormones. No published human trial has tested a dissolving microneedle patch for hair growth.
quick.mechanism: Dissolving needles penetrate the outer skin layer, then dissolve and release their payload into the skin. Laboratory and small human studies of such patches have examined delivery depth, stability and skin reactions.
quick.risks: A small human study of placebo dissolving patches found them well tolerated, with only mild redness that resolved. Microneedling in general can cause redness, bleeding and, with non-sterile tools, infection. Safety data for scalp hair products specifically were not found.

lead: Microneedle patches are arrays of microscopic needles, typically tens to a few hundred micrometres long, that pierce the outer skin and deliver a drug into it. Dissolving versions are made of water-soluble materials that dissolve in the skin, so nothing needs to be removed afterwards.[5][6] In hair-loss communities the terms nanoneedling or microneedle patches are used for products said to deliver actives such as minoxidil to the scalp, as a way to get more of the active into the skin without a clinic visit or an injection.

The idea sits next to a better-studied practice: microneedling the scalp with a roller or pen, usually combined with topical minoxidil. Randomized trials of that practice in androgenetic alopecia, including a 100-man trial from 2013 and a 60-man trial from 2020, reported larger hair-count or density gains with microneedling added than with minoxidil alone.[12][13] A 2018 systematic review lists hair loss among the conditions microneedling has been studied for.[14]

Published research on dissolving patches themselves covers delivery of methotrexate for psoriasis in a preclinical model, human growth hormone, insulin in diabetic rats, influenza vaccine in a human study, and mRNA formulations.[1][2][4][5][7][8][9] No study among those found tested a dissolving patch on hair growth. Wikipedia notes that the claim that microneedling may promote hair growth rests on weak sourcing.[11]

paras: Microneedles are grouped as solid, hollow, coated, dissolving and hydrogel-forming types. Dissolving types have tips that dissolve in the skin and may have incomplete insertion or slow dissolution [11]. A layered pyramidal design with flexible pedestals has been reported to improve delivery [7].

Wikipedia traces the concept of microneedles to hypodermic needles in the 1970s, with real prominence from the 1990s as microfabrication improved. In 1994 Orentreich described needle insertion into skin that appeared to stimulate fibrous strand release, an early step toward collagen induction therapy, and a 1998 Georgia Institute of Technology paper from the group of Mark Prausnitz showed microneedles can cross the stratum corneum for drug delivery.[11] Later work developed dissolving, coated, hollow and hydrogel-forming types.[11]

The aim of any microneedle design is to cross the stratum corneum, the outermost 10 to 15 micrometre layer, without reaching the nerves deeper in the tissue, which is why the procedure is described as causing little or no pain.[11] Dissolving needles release their payload as they dissolve; in an insulin study in rats, starch and gelatin needles dissolved within 5 minutes of insertion and reached about 200 micrometres depth.[4]

For hair, two mechanisms are proposed by supporters: better delivery of a topical drug through the skin barrier, and stimulation from the controlled micro-injury. A 2020 letter reported that microneedling improved minoxidil response in androgenetic alopecia patients by upregulating follicular sulfotransferase enzymes, the enzymes that convert minoxidil into its active form.[15]

In a 2013 randomized, evaluator-blinded pilot study of 100 men with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia, weekly microneedling plus twice-daily 5% minoxidil was compared with minoxidil alone over 12 weeks. The mean hair-count change was 91.4 in the microneedling group and 22.2 with minoxidil alone, and 82 percent of microneedling patients versus 4.5 percent reported improvement above 50 percent.[12]

In a 2020 randomized trial of 60 Chinese men, 24 weeks of electrodynamic microneedling every two weeks, minoxidil alone, or both produced mean hair density gains of 23.4, 18.8 and 38.3 per square centimetre respectively, with a significant difference between groups and no significant difference in toxicity.[13] A 2015 case series described four men who had not responded to finasteride and minoxidil and who improved after microneedling.[16] These studies used rollers or pens, not dissolving patches.
No studies found on dissolving microneedle patches for hair growth.

Related human work exists in other fields. A study of fifteen volunteers using placebo dissolving patches reported good tolerability with no pain or swelling and only mild redness that resolved.[3] A clinical study assessed influenza vaccination with a dissolving patch,[5] and stability work found influenza vaccine stable in such patches over long storage.[6] Preclinical research includes methotrexate for psoriasis,[1] human growth hormone,[2] insulin in diabetic rats,[4] caffeine in obese mice[8] and mRNA.[9] Meloxicam patches were formulated for arthritis.[10]
For microneedling with rollers or pens, randomized trials in androgenetic alopecia are described under Effectiveness.[12][13]

In general microneedling can cause redness, swelling, pinpoint bleeding and bruising, and non-sterile devices can lead to infection or pigmentation changes [11]. Placebo dissolving patches were well tolerated in a small human study [3].

Hair-loss users and sellers describe patches as a way to deliver actives to the scalp without an injection, and scalp microneedling is a widespread add-on to minoxidil routines. Marketing of hair patches draws on the published patch research in other fields, which was not designed to test hair outcomes.

timeline.event: Orentreich describes needle-induced stimulation of fibrous strand release in skin.[11]
A Georgia Tech study showed microneedles can penetrate the stratum corneum.[11]
A dissolving patch for human growth hormone delivery is reported.[2]
Randomized pilot trial of microneedling plus minoxidil in androgenetic alopecia.[12]
A human tolerability study of placebo dissolving patches is published.[3]
Randomized trial of electrodynamic microneedling with minoxidil in Chinese men.[13]

chain: Needles cross the outer skin layer of the scalp
Actives such as minoxidil are delivered into the skin, and the micro-injury itself is thought by proponents to stimulate follicles
angle.text: Proponents use microneedle patches and scalp microneedling to improve delivery of hair actives and to stimulate the scalp. Hair outcomes have been measured in microneedling trials, not yet in dissolving-patch trials.
